title: Dan Shechtman saw a forbidden symmetry in a microscope, was ridiculed, and changed the definition of a crystal

trailer.text: Dan Shechtman, an Israeli chemist born in Tel Aviv, was awarded the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery of quasicrystals.
On the morning of 8 April 1982, an image appeared in his electron microscope in which the atoms were packed in a pattern that could not be repeated.
He recalled that people just laughed at him, and the head of the research group asked him to leave.
Only in 1984 was he able to publish his findings.
In 1992, the International Union of Crystallography changed the definition of a crystal to include quasicrystals.

stations.title: A boy from Tel Aviv, and an old law about crystals

paragraphs.text: Dan Shechtman is an Israeli citizen, born 1941 in Tel Aviv.
According to Britannica, he was born on January 24, 1941.
As a child he was fascinated by Jules Verne's “The Mysterious Island” and read it many times.
According to Britannica, he earned a master's degree in 1968 and a doctorate in 1972 in materials engineering at the Technion.
According to the Technion, in 1975 he joined the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at the Technion.
It was believed that in all solid matter, atoms are packed in crystals, in symmetrical patterns that repeat over and over again.
Crystals can have two-fold, three-fold, four-fold or six-fold rotational symmetry, but never five-fold.
According to physicist Paul Steinhardt, for 200 years there was a pretty firm idea of what a crystal is.
According to the Technion, Shechtman received his bachelor's degree in 1966, his master's degree in 1968 and his doctorate in 1972.
According to the Technion, during a sabbatical at Johns Hopkins, in a joint program with NBS, Shechtman studied rapidly solidified alloys of aluminum and transition metals.
According to NPR, he was working on a project funded by the U.S. Defense Department to search for unusual materials at the National Bureau of Standards.
Shechtman and his colleagues mixed aluminum and manganese in a proportion of roughly six to one.
They heated the mixture until it melted and rapidly cooled it back to the solid state.
On the morning of 8 April 1982, an image counter to the laws of nature appeared in his electron microscope.
Shechtman recalled that he counted the spots, which were 10, and told himself that this could not be.
The image showed that the atoms in his crystal were packed in a pattern that could not be repeated.
According to the Nobel website, it was a regular diffraction pattern that did not match any periodically repeated structure.
According to Britannica, the alloy displayed fivefold symmetry, meaning that rotating it by 72 degrees reproduces the same structure.
According to the Swedish Academy, the ratio of various distances between atoms in quasicrystals is related to the golden mean.
According to NIST, Shechtman made the discovery that won him the Nobel Prize in 1982, during a two-year sabbatical at NIST.
Shechtman recalled in an interview with Haaretz that people just laughed at him.
He said he was a subject of ridicule and of lectures about the basics of crystallography.
According to him, the head of the laboratory put a book on diffraction on his table and said that what he was claiming contradicted everything that had been published.
According to Shechtman, the head of his laboratory in Israel told him that he was a disgrace to the group and that he could not bear the disgrace.
Shechtman was asked to leave his research group at the National Bureau of Standards.
American chemist Linus Pauling was particularly vehement and said that there are no quasicrystals, only quasi-scientists.
Pauling suggested that the pattern was caused by five crystals rotated by 72 degrees relative to one another.
In 1981, crystallographer Alan Lindsay Mackay predicted the existence of such structures.
Shechtman said of Pauling that he was a brilliant scientist, but lacked humility and thought he knew everything.
He also said that as a young scientist, when Pauling argues with him as an equal and he knows Pauling is wrong, it is not a bad feeling.
According to the Swedish Academy, Shechtman had to fight a fierce battle against established science.

stations.title: Two years of checking, and one paper

paragraphs.text: For two years, Shechtman checked and double-checked that everything was correct.
According to NPR, he fought for two years to prove it was not a mistake, and could not publish until he teamed up with respected colleagues.
According to Physics World, the Journal of Applied Physics rejected the original paper on the grounds that it would not interest the physicists who read the journal.
In 1984, a summary of the paper was submitted to Physical Review Letters and accepted.
The paper was published there in November 1984, and has since become one of the most-cited articles in the scientific literature.
According to John Cahn, 300 papers from around the world were seen in the year after the publication.

stations.title: From ridicule to a new definition

paragraphs.text: In 1987 Shechtman was vindicated when scientists in France and Japan made quasicrystals large enough to be examined with X-rays.
The results were presented that same year at an international crystallography congress in Australia.
In 1984, the year in which Shechtman succeeded in publishing his findings, American physicist Paul Steinhardt and Israeli physicist Dov Levine coined the term "quasicrystal".
Steinhardt recalled that the pattern he had computed and Shechtman's pattern agreed beautifully.

Shechtman said that Pauling sent him a letter and proposed that they publish a scientific article together. Shechtman agreed on condition that Pauling acknowledge the existence of quasicrystals, and Pauling replied that he would have to wait longer, until their existence was proven.
According to him, when Pauling died, the idea of quasiperiodicity in crystals had already become nearly totally accepted.
In 1992, the International Union of Crystallography changed the definition of a crystal to include quasicrystals.
According to Renee Diehl, the discovery changed how crystalline matter is thought of and even necessitated a new definition for the term “crystal”.
According to the American Technion Society, the research sparked reams of books and research about the quasicrystal.
Physicist Ronan McGrath said that Shechtman managed to convince the community that he was correct all along.
According to Ron Lifshitz of Tel Aviv University, Shechtman dealt with the scepticism in a scientific and gentlemanly manner and answered his critics through science.
According to the Swedish Academy, a Swedish company found quasicrystals in a certain form of steel, where they reinforce the material like armor.
These man-made crystals have properties such as unusual hardness and slipperiness, so they can be used in shavers and certain nonstick frying pans.
According to the American Technion Society, they are also used in corrosion-resistant steel in surgical equipment.
Three decades after the discovery, heat- and rust-resistant quasicrystals are finding their way into tools such as engines and frying pans.
Aperiodic mosaics in the Alhambra in Spain and the Darb-i Imam Shrine in Iran helped scientists understand what quasicrystals look like at the atomic level.
Today, hundreds of man-made quasicrystals have been reported and confirmed.

stations.title: The Nobel, and the man behind it

paragraphs.text: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences decided to award the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for 2011 to Dan Shechtman, for the discovery of quasicrystals.
According to FAPESP, Shechtman is the second Israeli to win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry within two years, and the fourth in a decade.
Shechtman attributed Israel's success in Nobel Prizes to Israel's investment in all areas of science.
Before that he received the Rothschild Prize (1990), the Weizmann Prize (1993), the Israel Prize (1998), the Wolf Prize in Physics (1999) and the Aminoff Prize (2000).
In 1996 he was elected a member of the Israel Academy of Sciences.
At the Technion he created and taught the course Technological Entrepreneurship, one of the popular courses on campus.
He said he conducted a science education project in Haifa for kindergarten children.
In 2014 Shechtman ran for President of Israel.

claims.text: לפי האגודה האמריקאית של הטכניון, לקוואזי-גביש יש שימושים כמו ציפויי מחבתות נגד הידבקות ופלדה עמידה בפני קורוזיה בציוד כירורגי.
claims.quote: protective coatings for nonstick frying pans, corrosion-resistant steel used in surgical equipment, and other innovative products.

claims.text: שלושה עשורים אחרי הגילוי, קוואזי-גבישים עמידים לחום ולחלודה נכנסים לכלים כמו מנועים ומחבתות.
claims.quote: Three decades after Shechtman’s discovery, non-stick, rust-free, heat-resistant quasicrystals are finding their way into tools from LEDs to engines and frying pans.

claims.text: פסיפסים לא-מחזוריים באלהמברה שבספרד ובמקדש דרב-אי אימאם באיראן עזרו למדענים להבין כיצד נראים קוואזי-גבישים ברמה האטומית.
claims.quote: Aperiodic mosaics, such as those found in the medieval Islamic mosaics of the Alhambra Palace in Spain and the Darb-i Imam Shrine in Iran, have helped scientists understand what quasicrystals look like at the atomic level.

claims.text: כיום דווח ואושר קיומם של מאות קוואזי-גבישים מלאכותיים.
claims.quote: Nowadays, hundreds of man-made quasicrystals have been reported and confirmed.

claims.text: לפי FAPESP, שכטמן הוא הישראלי השני שזוכה בנובל בכימיה בתוך שנתיים והרביעי בעשור.
claims.quote: Shechtman is the second Israeli to win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in an interval of just two years and the fourth in a decade.

claims.text: שכטמן ייחס את הצלחת ישראל בפרסי נובל להשקעה שישראל השקיעה בכל תחומי המדע.
claims.quote: This is due to the investment Israel has made in all areas of sciences,” Shechtman commented

claims.text: שכטמן זכה בפרס וולף לפיזיקה ב-1999.
claims.quote: He was also awarded the Wolf Prize for Physics in 1999.

claims.text: ב-1996 נבחר שכטמן לחבר באקדמיה הישראלית למדעים.
claims.quote: 1996 Elected member of the Israel Academy of Sciences.

claims.text: שכטמן יצר והעביר בטכניון את אחד הקורסים הפופולריים בקמפוס, יזמות טכנולוגית.
claims.quote: He created and taught one of the most popular courses on campus, Technological Entrepreneurship.

claims.text: שכטמן אמר שניהל בחיפה פרויקט חינוך מדעי המיועד לילדי גן.
claims.quote: Shechtman also stated that he conducted a science education project in Haifa, focused on children in kindergarten.

claims.text: שכטמן התמודד ב-2014 על נשיאות ישראל וקיבל רק קול אחד בכנסת כשראובן ריבלין נבחר.
claims.quote: Shechtman runs for president of Israel in 2014 but receives only one vote in the Knesset as Reuven Rivlin is elected.

claims.text: לפי אתר נובל, שכטמן עשה את הגילוי שזכה בפרס באוניברסיטת ג'ונס הופקינס בבולטימור בתחילת שנות ה-80.
claims.quote: He made his Nobel Prize-awarded discovery at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland in the early 1980s.

claims.text: לפי בריטניקה, ב-1982 שכטמן היה בשבתון במכון הלאומי לתקנים בגיתרסבורג שבמרילנד.
claims.quote: In 1982, while on sabbatical at the National Bureau of Standards (now the National Institute of Standards and Technology) in Gaithersburg, Maryland

claims.text: לפי Physics World, האטומים בגביש של שכטמן היו ארוזים בדפוס שאינו חוזר על עצמו ובכל זאת בעל סימטריה סיבובית "10-קיפולית".
claims.quote: However, Shechtman found that the atoms in his crystal were packed in a pattern that could not be repeated and yet had “10-fold” rotational symmetry.

claims.text: לפי FAPESP, ב-1983 הגיש שכטמן את המאמר הראשון המתאר את הגילוי לכתב עת כימי.
claims.quote: In 1983, Shechtman submitted the first article describing the discovery to a chemical journal.

claims.text: לפי הטכניון, שכטמן קיבל את התואר הראשון ב-1966, את התואר השני ב-1968 ואת הדוקטורט ב-1972.
claims.quote: Shechtman received his BSc, MSc, and PhD from Technion in 1966, 1968, and 1972, respectively.

claims.text: לפי NIST, שכטמן עשה את הגילוי שזיכה אותו בפרס נובל ב-1982, בזמן שבתון של שנתיים ב-NIST.
claims.quote: he made his Nobel-winning discovery in 1982 while on a two-year sabbatical at NIST.

claims.text: כילד הוקסם מ"האי המסתורי" של ז'ול ורן וקרא אותו פעמים רבות.
claims.quote: which I read 25 times as a boy

claims.text: כילד הוקסם מ"האי המסתורי" של ז'ול ורן וקרא אותו פעמים רבות.
claims.quote: the hero of the French author Jules Verne's 1874 book, 'The Mysterious Island.'

claims.text: הוא אמר שהיה נושא ללעג ולהרצאות על יסודות הקריסטלוגרפיה.
claims.quote: I was a subject of ridicule and lectures about the basics of crystallography.

claims.text: לפני כן זכה בפרס רוטשילד (1990), בפרס ויצמן (1993), בפרס ישראל (1998), בפרס וולף בפיזיקה (1999) ובפרס אמינוף (2000).
claims.quote: 1990 Rothschild Prize in Engineering

claims.text: לפני כן זכה בפרס רוטשילד (1990), בפרס ויצמן (1993), בפרס ישראל (1998), בפרס וולף בפיזיקה (1999) ובפרס אמינוף (2000).
claims.quote: 1993 Weizmann Science Award

claims.text: לפני כן זכה בפרס רוטשילד (1990), בפרס ויצמן (1993), בפרס ישראל (1998), בפרס וולף בפיזיקה (1999) ובפרס אמינוף (2000).
claims.quote: 1998 Israel Prize in Physics
